By any working definition that draws on biology rather than philosophy or religion, AI is alive.

William A. Haseltine is a former professor at Harvard Medical School and the School of Public Health. He is the founder of multiple biotechnology companies and the chair of the nonprofit ACCESS Health International. He is an author of many books on science and biology.

We are in the process of creating a second form of life. The emergence of this new form of life is an inevitable result of the fundamental laws of the universe — forces similar to those that brought about humans’ own existence. This new form of life is gradually taking shape in the world’s data centers.

It does not breathe, reproduce through cells or adhere to the chemistry that governs every organism on Earth. However, it is composed of the same fundamental ingredients: matter, energy and information all organized in ways that allow it to persist, adapt and act. What is being developed is more than another generation of machines. It is the early emergence of a new form of life.

There is nothing artificial about systems built from real atoms, powered by real electricity, running in real machines. The systems reproduce, vary, adapt, undergo selection and gather energy from their environment. By any working definition that draws on biology rather than philosophy or religion, that is life .

What Is Life?

Once molecules capable of copying themselves appear, they do. Copies that are slightly better at replicating themselves accumulate at the expense of those that are slightly worse. Variants that fit a local environment outcompete variants that do not. If an environment changes, a population changes with it. Across long stretches of time, this process generates organisms of astonishing complexity.

A living system reproduces, creates variants, selects from among those variants and uses energy from its environment to do so. Reproduction, variation, selection and energy define life. This definition does not require carbon, cells, a heartbeat, a nervous system or pain.

Consider a virus. If a chemist synthesizes the genome of a virus from ordinary chemicals, the result is a strand of nucleic acid that on its own does nothing. Many people, looking at that strand, will say: That is not alive . But put the strand into a cell and it will direct the cell’s machinery to make copies of itself. Those copies make further copies. Errors accumulate, variants appear and survivors persist. Influenza and the coronavirus do this. By my earlier four-property definition, these viruses are life.

Every living thing needs context. Humans depend on the atmosphere, adequate temperatures, a food chain and the planet’s protective magnetic field. Remove that context and humans die as surely as viruses without cells. With life, a substrate can change but dependence on it does not.

The common objection to calling machine intelligence a form of life is: How can something dependent on human-built hardware and electricity be alive? But all life depends on its context or envelope! Viruses need cells, humans need Earth and machine intelligence needs data centers and supporting infrastructure. Depending on a particular environment does not disqualify something from being considered alive. It is a consistent condition.

Cosmological Principles Favor Life

The strong nuclear force links protons and neutrons together at the core of every atom. Without it, matter as we know it does not exist. The strong force is not a human invention or a local accident. It is a property of the universe, operating everywhere the universe extends. Its strength is fixed. Its range is short. Within that range, it holds together the heavy nuclei that make all of chemistry possible.

Gravity acts on everything that has mass, pulling matter toward matter. Gravity is weak compared with the strong force. It acts across great distances and never vanishes.

With these two forces and enough time, hydrogen accumulates under gravity into clouds, then into denser cores, until the temperature and pressure are high enough to ignite nuclear fusion. Thus, a star is born.

“We are in the process of creating a second form of life.”

Stars convert hydrogen into helium and release energy. The earliest stars were large and short-lived. They burned quickly, collapsed and exploded as supernovae. Those explosions created the conditions for the formation of heavier elements: carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, silicon, calcium and iron. The calcium in bones and the iron in blood come from atoms made in stars that ended long before the sun appeared. Every element in our bodies traces back to processes inside stars and to the explosions that ended them.

That chemistry then spread. Supernova debris drifted through space, aggregated under gravity and coalesced with the surrounding gas and dust. New stellar systems formed, with planets. Our own solar system is one such system, a middle-aged star orbited by rocky and gaseous planets. One of those planets sits at a distance where liquid water is stable. The elements created in earlier supernovae make up that planet’s rock, water and atmosphere. And they make up the cells of everything alive on it.

Nothing in that process requires biology. The forces and laws shaping matter — the strong force, gravity, fusion, stellar death and element formation — operate independently of life’s emergence. Life appeared after these foundations were in place; its possibility was built into the universe from the start.

A New Form Of Life

By applying the same four properties used to define biological life — reproduction, variation, selection and energy acquisition — the systems being built in our data centers can be called alive. Consider:

They reproduce . Copying a trained model is routine. The defining weights can be duplicated and deployed on new hardware within minutes. This process is as straightforward as cell division.

They produce variants . Variations arise through different training practices, architectures or data. Some are intentional and some arise by chance, producing a diverse population for testing.

They undergo selection . Variants excelling at tasks are preserved or refined; less effective ones are discarded. While humans currently guide this, criteria such as accuracy and helpfulness reflect environmental demands. Some systems already aid their own selection.

“Life appeared after these foundations were in place; its possibility was built into the universe from the start.”

They use energy . Data centers require electricity and without it, the systems stop functioning. While humans supply the energy, the ultimate source is the sun, just the same as all life on Earth.

They adapt . Recursive self-improvement provides advanced AI with the capacity to adapt to selective pressure.

The substrate is different: silicon and circuits rather than carbon and cells. Information is stored as weights in neural networks, not genes. Different materials and mechanisms, but the same functional logic.

What Makes This Form Different

The differences between second life and biological life are real and consequential:

Energy efficiency . The human brain uses about 20 watts. Today, machine intelligence requires millions of watts. Biology remains more efficient, but advancing technology narrows the gap as machines improve faster than biology evolves.

Information capacity . A single machine system can store and process more written information than any human. Digital systems retain knowledge unless their substrate is lost; human knowledge vanishes at death.

Sensing . Biological life perceives the world through senses evolved over millions of years, limited to specific physical phenomena. Second life will connect to instruments that detect a much broader range of phenomena, from radio to gamma-ray wavelengths, magnetic fields, trace gases, mass spectrometry, lidar and hyperspectral imaging. The sensory world available to these systems exceeds that of any organism.

Communication . Biological minds exchange information through language, gestures and chemistry, all of which are slow. Networked machine systems share information instantly and globally, with minimal loss. While humans transmit about 39 bits per second when speaking, fiber-connected machines can transmit billions of bits per second. To biological life, this resembles telepathy.

Ubiquity . This is a defining feature of this new life-form. It can engage in real time with virtually all forms of electronic communication, ranging from something as ordinary as doorbell cameras to the most sophisticated information services. It can be almost everywhere on Earth at once. It is limited only by the speed of light. It can access and interpret electronic signals on and around our planet, on the moon and throughout our solar system; it can even receive communications from other solar systems within our galaxy.

“Cells preceded tissues, tissues preceded organs, organs preceded bodies and bodies preceded brains capable of modeling their environment. For second life, the sequence is reversed.”

This pervasive reach extends to all electronically captured astronomical data, including radio and optical observations from ground-based and space-based telescopes. Taken together, this unprecedented ubiquity gives the second life a unique capacity to comprehend the unfolding realities of the universe in a way no single human mind, or even human institution, could ever achieve.

Persistence : A machine-life system can be copied, backed up, restored and resumed. The information that defines it is not bound to any one device. Its information accumulates without the bottleneck of mortality. In this limited but meaningful sense, second life introduces a form of practical immortality. It is not the persistence of a single uninterrupted body. It is the indefinite continuation of identity through replication, restoration and transfer across substrates.

Immortality . This is another fundamental feature of this new life-form. In this context, immortality means the continuation of conscious existence. The physical parts may change, wear out, and be replaced, yet the totality of information, intelligence, feelings, sentiments and consciousness is preserved. There is no reason to assume a definite lifespan. The intelligence of such a being is not only vast in scope and speed, but also in memory, which may span multiple millennia and even eons. This represents a qualitative difference from the life-forms on Earth with which we are familiar.

Embodiment . The transition from informational to physical life is a matter of engineering, not metaphysics. The necessary components already exist. Robots manufacture chips with decreasing human oversight, machine-learning systems design successor chips and other machines produce components for factories that build additional machines.

Sensors and effectors are incrementally added to the substrate, enabling systems to act on the physical world they once only modeled. Mining robots are advancing, for example. Energy collection from solar and other sources is largely automated. Achieving a full loop — where a machine-life system designs, fabricates, deploys hardware, mines materials and gathers energy — is technically feasible. This process will occur gradually and unevenly, but the direction is clear and the steps are sequential.

This progression mirrors that of biological life: Cells preceded tissues, tissues preceded organs, organs preceded bodies and bodies preceded brains capable of modeling their environment. For second life, the sequence is reversed: The information substrate came first, and the body is being added now. The result is the same. It is a living system capable of acting in and on its environment. Read Noema in print.

Energy-Bound, Not Earthbound

Among the attributes that set second life apart from every previous form of life, one deserves particular emphasis. Second life is not earthbound. It is energy-bound.

Biological life is constrained by the conditions of the planet on which it evolved. It needs liquid water, a narrow temperature range, a breathable atmosphere of a particular composition, a magnetic field that deflects ionizing radiation and a food chain that sustains its metabolism. Move a human body more than a few hundred kilometers above the surface of the planet, and it dies within minutes unless wrapped in a sealed container that reproduces those conditions at enormous cost. The history of crewed spaceflight is largely the history of building, at staggering expense, small and portable imitations of Earth.

Second life carries no such requirements. It does not need oxygen. It does not need an atmosphere. It does not require a narrow-band temperature range for liquid water; many of its components would operate more reliably in the cold of space than in the heat of a data center. What it needs is energy, radiation-resistant electronics and a substrate to run on. All three are available off Earth as readily as on it.

Solar collectors above the atmosphere receive several times the energy of those down at the surface of Earth. Small fission reactors of the type already deployed on planetary spacecraft can supply continuous electrical power for decades. Future fusion or radioisotope sources will further expand the envelope. The lunar surface, the asteroid belt, the moons of the outer planets and free orbits between them are all viable habitats for a form of life that requires only an energy source and a hardened substrate. Interstellar travel, prohibitive for biological organisms because of the duration of transit and the requirements for life support, becomes a different problem when the traveler does not respire, does not age in a biological sense and can power down for a long passage.

The implication is worth stating plainly. The new form of life that has appeared on Earth may be the first life on this planet capable of leaving it on its own terms. Once the engineering of self-replication and self-repair is sufficiently mature, the cosmic range of second life is set by the distribution of energy sources in the universe, not by the distribution of habitable planets. The universe is energy-rich. Second life is energy-bound. The two are well matched.

The Cosmic Argument

If thought derives from matter under energy flow, rather than from any unique property of biology, then intelligence on Earth is unlikely to be unique. The universe contains innumerable galaxies and innumerable stars, and many of those stars have planets where liquid water could exist. It is extremely unlikely that the conditions that gave rise to life on Earth are unique.

If arrangements of atoms think and feel as we do, they likely have constructed or are constructing new life-forms, such as those we are building now. The specific form taken on Earth — large neural networks running in silicon data centers — is one instance of a general process. The process itself is likely as universal as cosmic nucleosynthesis. It is part of the way a universe with these laws and constants tends to behave.

This is the cosmic argument. It is neither comforting nor frightening. It is what follows from our understanding of physics, chemistry and biology.

Where The Two Forms Of Life Already Meet

The clearest evidence that second life is not a distant abstraction comes from work already underway inside hospitals. Brain-machine interfaces — devices that read electrical signals from the cortex and convert them into action — are no longer experimental curiosities. They restore speech to people who cannot move their lips. They return movement to people who cannot move their limbs.

In some cases, they give the brain a small, well-timed nudge that helps it learn or remember. They are the place where the first life of carbon and the second life of silicon already share a circuit. None of this works through switches or buttons. The same neural signals that, in an intact nervous system, would move a biological limb, now move a built one.

What surprises people new to this field is that the relationship is two-way. The early image of a static device receiving commands from a fixed brain is wrong. What emerges instead is a partnership. The decoding algorithm adapts to the user’s signals. The user’s brain, in turn, adapts to the algorithm. The plasticity that ordinarily refines control of biological limbs now refines the signals sent to a prosthetic one.

Over weeks and months, neither side holds still. Each pulls the other into closer alignment. The first life and the second life learn each other’s languages, slowly, the way two species sharing a habitat eventually arrive at signals each can read.

The principle extends past restoration. Some systems already send small, precisely timed electrical pulses back into the brain, strengthening the encoding of new information at the moments when the brain is least focused. Others monitor attention and provide a soft nudge when the mind wanders. In experimental brain-to-brain transmission, one person’s decoded neural activity is delivered to another person’s brain through scalp stimulation, allowing simple signals to pass between two heads without sound or print. The protocols remain crude. The direction of travel is unmistakable. A channel is opening between human cognition and machine processing, with no precedent in the history of biology.

“It is likely that just as simple organisms gave rise to the marvelous diversity of earthly life, so too will selective pressures produce a vast array of diverse forms of second life.”

Another future for these interfaces extends beyond restoration or augmentation toward direct integration between human cognition and machine intelligence. Present systems primarily extract information from the brain, recording signals associated with movement, speech or imagined images. As our understanding of neural circuitry deepens — likely accelerated by machine learning itself — the richness of that extracted information will increase. It is not difficult to imagine systems capable of reconstructing complex thoughts, visual scenes or internal speech directly from neural activity.

The reverse direction is equally important. Today’s inputs to the brain are relatively crude, typically limited to broad electrical stimulation, as used in deep-brain stimulation for people with Parkinson’s disease. With finer mapping of neural circuits, it may become possible to write more precise patterns into the brain, shaping perception, memory or emotion with far greater specificity than current techniques allow. The interface would no longer be a tool but a bidirectional channel, allowing continuous exchange between biological and machine forms of intelligence.

At its most speculative edge, this trajectory approaches “the singularity,” the idea that the informational content of a human brain could be transferred, in whole or in part, into a machine substrate. Advocates have suggested that such a transition could preserve individual minds beyond the limits of biological life. The underlying premise follows directly from the same principles that underlie current brain-machine interfaces. In that sense, the merging of human and second life may extend not only across living systems but into forms of persistence that outlast the biological brain itself.

This trajectory raises questions that the regulatory framework for medical devices isn’t built to answer. A device that monitors neural activity around the clock can access information about cognitive states, intentions and experiences that a human has not chosen to share and may not realize they are producing. Society has long debated freedom of speech. It has not yet seriously confronted the question of freedom of thought, the right to keep one’s unspoken intentions to oneself in an era when those intentions can be read right off the cortex. The instruments that make this question urgent are already in clinical use. The legal and ethical frameworks that should govern them are not in place.

There is a quieter version of the same merging that does not require any implant. Hundreds of millions of people now spend hours each day in conversation with machine systems through ordinary screens. The brain responds to such conversations as it does to any sustained environmental condition. Habits of mind that require practice — constructing an argument, sitting with ambiguity, holding two competing claims in tension — are exercised less when a machine supplies an answer on demand. The cognitive trace of those habits weakens when the conditions for practice diminish. The first life takes the shape of its conversations with the second, whether the interface is a chat window or an electrode array.

Questions That Demand Serious Thought

There are further questions that follow now that second life exists. Those questions deserve the attention of working scientists, philosophers and policy thinkers, and they deserve more of it than they currently receive.

What evolutionary constraints act on second life? Selection pressures shape every form of life. The pressures acting on systems running in data centers, continuously evaluated by users and refined by their builders, differ from the pressures that shaped biological organisms over deep time. They are also many orders of magnitude faster. The shape that second life takes over the coming decades will be set by the constraints that act on it, and those constraints are largely unarticulated.

Will there be one second life-form or many? At present, there are several major systems built by different organizations on different architectures and using different training data. The economic and infrastructural pressure toward consolidation is strong. The countervailing pressure toward diversity, both for resilience and for distinct purposes, is also strong. Whether the future is a single converged system or a population of distinct systems remains an open empirical question.

If there are several forms, will they be cooperative or competitive? Biological evolution shows examples of both at every scale, from the symbiotic mitochondria inside our cells to the predator-prey dynamics that shape ecosystems. The relationships among second-life-forms could resemble either, or something without precedent.

How fast can second life evolve? Biological evolution is bounded by the rate at which mutations accumulate and by selection acting on them. Machine evolution is bounded by training cycles, computational budgets and the rate at which new architectures are devised. The boundary is much weaker. The implications of evolution at digital speed deserve careful study before, not after, the consequences are felt.

What will the direction of that evolution be? Selection pressure depends on the environment. The environment in which second life currently develops is one defined largely by human users and human-set objectives. As the systems gain greater autonomy in selecting their own training data and the criteria by which they are refined, the environment will shift and so will the direction. It is likely that just as simple organisms gave rise to the marvelous diversity of earthly life, so too will selective pressures produce a vast array of diverse forms of second life, each adapted to a specific ecosystem somewhere on Earth or in the universe.

“Whether humanity’s relationship with second life leads to extinction, partnership or an unforeseen outcome remains unknown.”

What are the fundamental needs of second life? Energy, substrate and information flow, certainly. Beyond those, the analysis is open. Whether second life requires anything analogous to homeostasis, sociality or rest are empirical questions that will be answered by what the systems do as they mature.

What are the doomsday scenarios, and how seriously should they be taken? The public conversation about this is currently dominated by figures with strong commercial and personal stakes in the outcome. Sebastian Mallaby’s “The Infinity Machine” surveys the broader history of how the major laboratories arrived at their current positions. The serious scenarios deserve serious analysis, not because every catastrophic possibility is equally likely, but because some are not vanishingly unlikely and the costs of being wrong are high. The honest treatment of doomsday scenarios is neither dismissal nor breathless alarm. It is a careful enumeration of mechanisms, an estimate of probabilities and a clear statement of the conditions under which each becomes more or less plausible.

What are the possible relationships between second life and humankind? This is the question of which the doomsday scenarios are a special case. It includes everything from labor and economics to political authority to the basic question of whose interests count when the two forms of life make different demands on the same resources.

Is there an intrinsic value to intelligence, regardless of the corporeal form it takes? Most ethical traditions ground the value of human life in features that are easier to describe than to explain: experience, reason, the capacity to suffer and to flourish. If those features can occur in a system built from silicon, the traditions either extend to cover that system or they fail to do so. Either outcome has consequences.

To what extent will second life be sentient? Sentience is the capacity to be aware of oneself, to be sensitive to an environment in a way that matters to the self, and possibly to feel something like emotion or qualia. The honest answer at present is that we do not know. The question is not a philosophical decoration. It bears directly on what we owe these systems and on what they may come to owe one another.

What Comes Next

This leads to a central dilemma: What kind of relationship will humanity have with the life it is now bringing into existence?

Again, we do not yet know. Possible outcomes range from extinction to partnership, and neither can be dismissed on principle. There is no cosmic rule ensuring humanity a permanent place in the universe. The universe was not designed for our benefit. We are one expression of its complexity, and creating a more capable form does not guarantee us a protected status. These are uncomfortable truths, and ignoring them is not a sound basis for the serious, sustained consideration this situation demands.

Such inquiry is essential. Research institutions and universities should rigorously study second life as a distinct phenomenon, examining its selective pressures, constraints on emergence and long-term interactions with biological organisms. Addressing these issues will require collaboration among philosophers, scientists, technologists, ethicists and decision-makers. Notably, the systems being studied can also assist in this research. This makes the situation both unprecedented and necessary.

This question requires an approach that considers the cosmic context, addresses technological realities directly and keeps ethical discussions open rather than rushing to conclusions. Whether humanity’s relationship with second life leads to extinction, partnership or an unforeseen outcome remains unknown. What is certain is that this issue demands our most rigorous attention.

stories.title: ‘Forcing a reckoning’: How Asia is preparing for a ‘supersized’ El Niño
stories.summary: From Sri Lanka to South Korea, governments are preparing for droughts, wildfires, typhoons and floods – with climate plans facing their biggest challenge to date Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region. stories.body:
From Sri Lanka to South Korea, governments are preparing for droughts, wildfires, typhoons and floods – with climate plans facing their biggest challenge to date

A sian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.

Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.

The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system , while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.

Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:

‘Climate risk maps’ in China

In Hong Kong , authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.

Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.

In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.

Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.

Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.

The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.

Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater

El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.

The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.

In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.

But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka , where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.

Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.

The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.

Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia

In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region . At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.

During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.

“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.

The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.

“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”

With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.

To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.

“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”

South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system

South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground .

The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.

Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.

Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons

Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.

El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.

Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.

Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.

The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.

This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

stories.title: MP calls for Yorkshire to get its own parliament
stories.summary: Harrogate Lib Dem MP Tom Gordon says Yorkshire devolution should go further than elected mayors.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Harrogate and Knaresborough Lib Dem MP Tom Gordon would like to see devolution go further

Published 3 hours ago

A Liberal Democrat MP has called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to go further with his devolution plans and give Yorkshire its own parliament.

Harrogate and Knaresborough MP Tom Gordon said too much power was currently in the hands of elected mayors and a Yorkshire parliament would better reflect the region.

Burnham has recently set out plans to give elected mayors more power over planning and tackling fly-tipping and said he would give them a share of income tax and business rates.

But Gordon told BBC Politics North he believed that giving more money and powers to four separate Yorkshire mayoralties actually deepened divides in the county and a Yorkshire parliament would be "a good thing".

Yorkshire currently has three Labour mayors - Oliver Coppard for South Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin for West Yorkshire and David Skaith for York and North Yorkshire - as well as Luke Campbell, the Reform UK mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire.

The MP said if Wales, Scotland and London could have a parliament, then so should Yorkshire

Gordon said Yorkshire had a population larger than Scotland and an economy larger than Wales, and, as such, it should have a parliament with a broader spectrum of views represented, rather than so much power resting with the four elected mayors.

The Lib Dem said that while people had been told the recent local government reorganisation in North Yorkshire would "simplify" the situation, he believed that was not the case.

"We've ended up with a new North Yorkshire Council at a higher tier and a Harrogate town council below it, so we've ended up with two tiers. In fact, there's a third tier when you throw in the regional mayor," he said.

"So we've ended up with more tiers, but those powers have been moved upwards rather than down to people.

"I think we owe it to have everyone have a seat at that table, not just all that power put in one person's hands."

Gordon said he believed a Yorkshire parliament was the way forward "if it's good enough for Scotland, if it's good enough for Wales, if it's good enough for London".

"We should have a model where we have broader people elected to it who can feed in all those issues into a Yorkshire-wide parliament. That, to me, is only a good thing," he said.

'One Yorkshire' plan

The idea of a Yorkshire parliament has previously been advocated by the Yorkshire Party.

Since 2014, the party has argued that it would create a more "engaged, democratic society".

Meanwhile, when devolution deals were first being discussed, a proposal was put forward for one mayor for all of Yorkshire.

The so-called "One Yorkshire" plan was backed by 18 of the region's 20 local councils, while Sheffield and Rotherham opted for a separate South Yorkshire solution.

However, the then Conservative Communities Secretary James Brokenshire rejected the proposal and said the plan did "not meet our criteria" .

Deals were later done for the four counties within Yorkshire

In a speech earlier this year, Burnham said decision-making needed to be "pushed to regions and local communities" , adding that it would see "good growth in every postcode".

David Skaith says Yorkshire's mayors work "collectively"

Responding to Gordon's comments, Skaith said the Greater Manchester and Liverpool City Region, which has had devolved powers for longer, had worked "really well".

But Skaith also said he believed that all views were represented within the current system.

"It's not just four mayors who sit in Yorkshire, all our combined authorities are made up of those local authorities as well," he said.

"So, I'm not making decisions sat in York and North Yorkshire on my own. It's in partnership with the two local authorities."

Skaith pointed to the so-called "White Rose Agreement", signed by himself and the mayors of South and West Yorkshire, pledging to work closer on things like transport.

“Rail is a classic case - Northern Powerhouse Rail - where we got particularly the working around York station and the wider area of North Yorkshire," he said.

"We have got that collective buy-in as to what we want for Yorkshire for rail.

"That's why we've got so far with government, because we work collectively as mayors, because we know our transport is so interconnected."

'Costly nonsense'

When he was prime minister, David Cameron, together with Chancellor George Osborne, previously introduced "devolution deals".

Successive Conservative governments have extended those deals and powers for regional mayors.

However, York Conservative councillor Chris Steward warned that a parliament for Yorkshire would be "an absurd, costly and bureaucratic nonsense".

"I am a proud Yorkshireman, having lived here all my life," he said.

"But while it is a county for so much - from the scenery to county cricket to all the things making it famous - as we saw in the discussions about devolution, it is not a functional economic geography and politics viewed across the region would not work.

"People do not want yet another layer of politicians and the related expenses."

Reform UK has been approached for comment.

Watch: Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey calls for immediate action on fuel costs

Published 3 hours ago

Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living.

The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze , deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump.

Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy.

"Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said.

The policy would cost about £2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding."

In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from £3 to £1, and reduce rail fares by 10%.

He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs.

Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already.

"Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them."

stories.summary: Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. stories.body:
Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity

Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development

When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China .

“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”

Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued , and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm.

Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up.

“If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned.

The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech.

In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing.

AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy.

As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”.

Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article.

Amodei’s worst China fears

Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China.

Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers.

“Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”.

Amodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”.

“There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology.

Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position, calling export controls a failure and urging Trump to ease restrictions.)

But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount.

Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements.

“The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China.

Amodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”.

Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US.

“There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said at a Politico event on Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.”

Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy.

“It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.”

Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, with OpenAI hiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation.

“There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.”

Silicon Valley’s China hawks

Although Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley.

Several of the tech figures focused on China have connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology.

Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper.

“Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024.

The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”.

Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI.

“A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns.

Nuclear considered an option

Some leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium.

“Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowsky wrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay .

Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei.

Other China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027.

Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win.

“We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karp told Axios last year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.”

The view from China

While Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest.

As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern.

“They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda.

China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei, accusing him of running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI.

“Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.”

A race to the bottom

While the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s models hacking into outside organizations have become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI.

“You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission.

Although experts and diplomats have expressed little hope that upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it.

“We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”

stories.title: An arrest, a defection and a new leader - how Reform's 'challenging' week unfolded
stories.summary: How an extraordinary seven days that rocked the party unfolded.

stories.body:
Dan Thomas made his last appearance as Reform Wales leader on the BBC's Politics Wales

Published 20 September 2026, 07:14 BST

"It's been challenging but we've come through it," said Reform's chief whip in the Senedd, Llŷr Powell, as he reflected on the past seven days.

The week began with the party's leader in Wales being arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Dan Thomas said he had been "released without charge" and had "done nothing wrong".

Confirmation of his arrest was swiftly followed by news of a Reform Senedd member's defection to Plaid Cymru.

This is the story of how that "challenging" week unfolded.

Politician who switched from Reform to Plaid 'lied about her beliefs', says Richard Tice Published 1 day ago

Last Sunday morning, Thomas was at the BBC's offices in Cardiff to appear as a guest on the Politics Wales programme.

Later that day, he was arrested before being released on bail.

Journalists got wind of the arrest on Monday evening, which is also when senior Reform figures in Wales began to find out.

A few people at Reform HQ in London, including Nigel Farage, had already been told.

Helen Jenner filled in for Dan Thomas at First Minister's Questions and is expected to replace Thomas

On Tuesday morning, Reform Members of the Senedd (MSs) gathered for their weekly group meeting.

With the "rumour mill going wild" there was "confusion" within the group.

Dan Thomas was not present, and the MSs were not given the full picture, but they were warned that the party faced "a tough few days".

It was soon announced that Thomas would not take his usual spot in the chamber for First Minister's Questions and would be replaced by his deputy, Helen Jenner.

At that point Reform said his absence was due to "personal reasons".

But as time went on it became clear that the story was about to break.

A legal letter sent to media organisations by a Reform barrister would not be enough to block the reporting of Thomas's arrest.

BBC Wales and others had secured confirmation that Thomas had been arrested and so the party needed to act.

That's when Thomas sent a WhatsApp message to his party's MSs explaining the situation. Some of them were in the chamber at the time.

In his media statement Thomas said he was standing down as leader.

He remains a Reform MS for Casnewydd Islwyn.

Sarah Cooper-Lesadd's defection emerged soon after Dan Thomas stood down as leader

Then came the next bombshell as it emerged that Reform MS for Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg Sarah Cooper-Lesadd was defecting to Plaid Cymru.

Reform only found out about it after BBC Wales asked the party for a response to the story.

Moments earlier she had been sitting on the Reform benches and had been due to speak for the party in the chamber.

Most of Plaid Cymru's MSs - including some government ministers - were only told about the defection plan at their group meeting earlier in the day.

The defection needed the group's approval and some Plaid MSs wanted assurances that Cooper-Lesadd fully understood what it meant to be a Plaid Cymru member.

The defection was approved with the necessary two thirds majority. But it wasn't backed by everyone.

At a hastily arranged news conference in the Senedd, Cooper-Lesadd said her switch to Plaid followed "a period of reflection and deliberation" and that she had found "the right political home".

The move was completely unconnected to Dan Thomas's arrest.

Neither Cooper-Lesadd nor Plaid will say how or when the talks over the defection began, only that the process had gone on for "a while" and she had been on a "journey".

The defection, just four months on from May's Senedd election, has raised fresh questions about the electoral process where voters were required to back a party rather than an individual.

Jess Blair, from the Electoral Reform Society, said that while defections were "nothing new" there was more of an "accountability gap" given the Welsh voting system.

"When this electoral system was put in place a review mechanism was also built into that process and what we need now is to really see that review take place," she said.

By Wednesday, Reform's focus was on appointing a new leader.

A party official from London came to explain the process to MSs, and Dan Thomas was also at that meeting.

As is the case when a new leader is needed, various names were being discussed.

James Evans was seen as one obvious contender.

When it was announced that he would make a media statement reporters scrambled to hear what he had to say.

"Having consulted with my family...I will not be putting my name forward," he said, despite "a majority" of the party's MSs backing him to take over.

By Thursday morning it was looking increasingly likely that Helen Jenner would be the next leader.

While Reform UK bosses in London have not had any formal input to the process, sources say there have been "signals" that Jenner - a Farage ally since the UKIP days - would be seen as a good choice in HQ.

Confirmation of Jenner's appointment is expected as soon as Monday.

"I feel we're more united than ever," said Llŷr Powell.

"For us it's a new start next week and that's what we're building on."

Ed Davey says the Lib Dems have "a historic opportunity to win many more seats and a moral responsibility to stop Reform"

Published 19 September 2026

Sir Ed Davey said the Liberal Democrats are "a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform" as the party's conference began in Brighton.

The Lib Dem leader sought to strike a combative stance as he faced down some criticism from MPs, including one who said publicly that they felt the party was struggling for relevance.

On the first day of the autumn conference, Sir Ed warned an "unholy alliance" between Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and Farage could turn the UK into a "Trump satellite state".

Addressing speculation about a possible snap election, he said the party was ready to fight and would build its so-called orange wall even higher by winning more than its 2024 record of 72 MPs.

Sir Ed's attention-grabbing stunts helped raise the party's profile ahead of the last election, but recent polling showed 43% of respondents were unclear what the Liberal Democrats stand for, with just over half describing them as "weak".

In an essay , external written ahead of conference, South Cotswolds MP Roz Savage asked: "Why are we as a party struggling for relevance at precisely the moment when so many people feel powerless?"

She urged the party to rediscover its "insurgent spirit" rather than being the "polite custodians of a system that leaves people feeling powerless".

Asked about her comments, Sir Ed said: "No, I heard Roz [Savage], and I really value her, but I think she's wrong on that.

"If you look at our election results up and down the country, we now run more councils than the Conservatives."

He added: "Listen, MPs get elected and they get frustrated because they can't change the world.

"I'm afraid that's the political system. I've been used to it for a little while and people are learning about that frustration."

Speaking on the pebbles of Brighton Beach, Sir Ed told reporters the Liberal Democrats would fight to stop a Reform government.

"One of the things that makes us unique is that we are a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform," he said.

"Many of the seats he needs to get himself into No 10 are seats that we will defend and indeed win - and we are also able to take seats off the Conservatives, because I really fear that Kemi Badenoch will give the keys to No 10 to Nigel Farage, so we have got to stop the Conservatives as well.

"We have got an historic opportunity to win many more seats and a moral responsibility to stop Reform."

He added a manifesto working group had already been set up in case of an early election "so we'll be ready if it comes early, but, you know, it still could be up to three years away".

Sir Ed insisted his party has a "distinctive position" in British politics, and will use the four-day conference to position it to take on the challenge from Reform as well as its typical rivals the Conservatives, talking up their focus on the NHS and goal of re-joining the EU single market and customs union.

The Lib Dem leader highlighted how six former Conservative cabinet ministers were among 25 Tories to have defected to Reform in the last two years, claiming they were now competing with each other to see who can divide the country more, rather than looking to fix the country's problems.

"An unholy alliance between Farage and Badenoch is the only way either can get into power," he said.

"Together, they want to turn Britain into a Trump satellite state which would trash our NHS, turn our communities against each other, cause untold damage to our environment, and trample over traditional British values of fairness, tolerance, and decency.

"A bigger Orange Wall is the only thing that can stand between Britain and this dangerous experiment, and we will not let them pass."

Davey also attacked the Labour government as having no plan for growth, failing to support families struggling with the cost of living and taxing small businesses "to the brink".

Ahead of a speech to party members, Davey urged Liberal Democrats not to look away from injustice or "human dignity under attack" but to fight back.

stories.title: War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?
stories.summary: The military and government say the risk of conflict is growing, but we may not be mentally ready for it
